title: NMLS License Renewal: A Loan Officer's Year-End Checklist
description: NMLS renewal season is open. Here's a loan officer's checklist for the 8-hour CE rule, California DFPI requirements, deadlines, and avoiding a lapsed license.
image_alt: A person writing in a notebook at a gray desk workspace

faq.q: When is the NMLS renewal period for loan officers?
faq.a: NMLS lists the annual renewal period as November 1 through December 31. A reinstatement period runs January 1 through the end of February, if your state allows it, but your license isn't active until it's reinstated.

faq.q: How many hours of continuing education do MLOs need each year?
faq.a: At least eight hours of NMLS-approved CE: three hours of federal law, two of ethics, two of nontraditional mortgage lending, and one elective, which some states such as California require to be state-specific.

faq.q: Can I take the same CE course I took last year?
faq.a: No. According to NMLS, the SAFE Act prohibits taking the same course in successive years, so choose a different approved course each year.

body_html:
Every year, somewhere around December 30, a loan officer logs into NMLS and realizes their continuing education never posted. The courses were finished. The certificate is sitting in their inbox. But the provider hadn't reported it yet, the renewal can't move, and January 1 is a day away. It's one of the most avoidable problems in this business, and it still catches good people.

The annual renewal window is open right now, so this is the right week to deal with it. Here's the checklist I'd want every loan officer on my team to run through, plus a few habits that turn renewal season into something more useful than paperwork.

How the NMLS renewal window works

According to the NMLS Annual Renewal Overview for Individuals, the renewal period runs from November 1 through December 31 each year. During that window you submit your renewal request, complete your attestation, and pay the NMLS processing fee plus any state fees.

Submitting is not the same as being renewed. Your state regulator reviews the request and looks at whether you've met your continuing education and background check requirements before approving it. If you miss the window, NMLS runs a reinstatement period from January 1 through the end of February, but reinstatement depends on your state allowing it, and in the meantime your license isn't active. For a working loan officer, that means files that can't move.

Your 8 hours of CE, broken down

The NMLS continuing education FAQ spells out the federal minimum: at least eight hours of approved CE every year. Those hours have to cover specific subjects:

RequirementHoursWhat it covers
Federal law and regulations3RESPA, TILA, ECOA, the SAFE Act and related rules
Ethics2Fraud, consumer protection, and fair lending
Nontraditional mortgage lending2Lending standards for nontraditional products
Elective or state-specific1Often a state law course, depending on your regulator

That last hour matters in California. The NMLS page for California DFPI requirements lists one hour of DFPI-specific education as part of the eight, and notes that DFPI-licensed loan officers can't renew without completing CE. If you hold licenses in multiple states, each one can have its own state elective, so check every regulator you're licensed with, not just your home state.

Two rules trip people up more than they should:

  • No repeats. The NMLS FAQ is clear that the SAFE Act prohibits taking the same course in successive years. Grabbing last year's package again can leave you short.
  • CE counts toward the year you take it. Courses completed in 2026 are what renew you for 2027. Hours taken in January don't fix a December gap; that becomes a Late CE situation with its own rules.

A year-end renewal checklist

Here's the order I'd tackle it in. Most of this takes less than an hour once the courses are done.

  1. Log into NMLS and look at your CE record. Confirm what's posted, not what you think you took.
  2. Book your courses now. Pick an approved provider and finish the eight hours early in the window. Providers need time to report completions to NMLS, and the last two weeks of December are when everyone else is trying to do the same thing.
  3. Verify the credit posted. A few days after finishing, check your NMLS record again. If it's missing, contact the provider while there's still time to fix it.
  4. Review your disclosures. Make sure your NMLS record is accurate and current before you attest. Changes in address, employment, or disclosure answers need to be updated, not glossed over.
  5. Submit the renewal and pay the fees. Do it well before the holidays. Keep the confirmation.
  6. Watch for regulator deficiencies. Regulators can post deficiencies to your record. Check back until your license shows as approved for the new year.

If you lead a team, put this on a shared calendar for every licensed person, with a check-in in mid-November and again in early December. One expired license on a team creates problems for everyone working those files.

Use CE as real training, not a checkbox

I'll be honest about something: most loan officers treat CE as eight hours of clicking through slides. That's a missed opportunity. The federal law hours touch the exact rules that shape how you advertise, disclose, and talk to borrowers. The ethics hours cover fair lending, which should inform every conversation you have.

A few ways to get more out of it:

  • Choose live or instructor-led courses when you can. You'll remember more, and you can ask questions about real scenarios.
  • Take notes on one thing to change. Maybe it's how you word a social post, or how you document a conversation about loan options.
  • Bring it back to the team. A ten-minute recap in a team meeting turns one person's CE into everyone's refresher.

The habits that make a strong first year, which I wrote about in A New Loan Officer's First 90 Days, don't stop after year one. Learning something new every week is what keeps a career growing, and CE is a built-in reason to do it.

Renewal season is also a career check-in

The end of the year is a natural time to ask bigger questions. Are you getting the training and support you need? Do you have access to the loan programs your clients and agents actually ask for? Is your team culture making you better, or just keeping you busy?

If the answers point toward a change, plan it carefully. Your individual license lives in NMLS, but originating for a new company requires that company to sponsor your license and your regulator to approve the relationship. Timing a move around renewal season, with your CE done and your record clean, makes that process smoother. If you're weighing different paths, my post on why more loan officers are choosing the broker channel walks through what that model looks like.

Whatever you decide, the loan officers who grow fastest are the ones who treat their license, their education, and their team as investments rather than obligations. That's the kind of culture I care about building.

The takeaway

Renewal season rewards the people who start early. Finish your eight hours this month, confirm they posted in NMLS, check your state-specific requirement, and submit your renewal before the holiday rush. Then use the time you saved to think about where you want your career to be a year from now.

If you're a loan officer in Southern California and you want to talk about training, mentorship, or what a supportive team looks like, I'm always happy to have that conversation.
